title: The 12 Week Year
author: Brian Moran & Michael Lennington
tagline: Most people take 12 months to do what they could do in 12 weeks — if they treated every week like it mattered.
oneLiner: Compress your year to 12 weeks and urgency returns. Vision, weekly plans, and accountability do the rest.
bigIdea: The problem with annual goals: 11 months of slack. Moran and Lennington's fix is brutal and effective — treat 12 weeks as one year: define a 12-week vision, break it into weekly plans, track lead (not lag) indicators on a public scoreboard, and meet a weekly accountability partner. When the 'year' is only 84 days long, urgency is automatic — and people consistently achieve in 12 weeks what they planned for 12 months.
quotes: The present moment is where the future is won or lost.
What you do today matters — because you're exchanging a day of your life for it.
Most people don't fail at execution; they fail at the system.

lessons.title: Compress Your Year: 12 Weeks, Not 12 Months
lessons.summary: Annual planning has a built-in failure: a 12-month horizon feels so far away that urgency never arrives until December. Compressing the 'year' to 12 weeks changes the psychology — you can see the finish line, deadlines feel real, and you get 4 'years' of learning and momentum per calendar year instead of one.
lessons.example: Moran's clients — from Fortune 500 teams to solo founders — routinely produce in one 12-week cycle what their annual plans promised for the year: a sales team Moran coached hit its yearly number in the first 12-week period.
lessons.action: Pick ONE goal you've been 'going to do this year.' Redefine it as a 12-week deadline: what exactly will be true 84 days from today?

lessons.title: Vision First, Then Goals
lessons.summary: Before goals, write your 12-week vision: a vivid, first-person description of your life and work at the end of the 12 weeks — who you are, what you've built, how it feels. The vision creates emotional pull; goals convert it into targets. A goal without a vision is a chore; a vision without goals is a daydream.
lessons.example: Moran's top performers write their vision as a letter to themselves dated 12 weeks out — then derive exactly 3–5 goals from it, each measurable ('I have 40,000 followers' or 'I've shipped the beta'), each tied to a number.
lessons.action: Write a 100-word letter from your future self, dated 84 days from today. Underline the three measurable results in it — those are your goals.

lessons.title: Lead Indicators Beat Lag Indicators
lessons.summary: Lag indicators (revenue, weight, sales) tell you the outcome — too late to change it. Lead indicators (calls made, workouts done, pages written) drive the outcome and can be executed this week. The 12 Week Year runs on weekly plans of lead actions: every Sunday, block your week with the specific actions that will move your goals.
lessons.example: A struggling sales team Moran coached stopped measuring 'deals closed' (lag) and started measuring 'qualified conversations' (lead) — within weeks, the lag number followed the lead number upward.
lessons.action: For each 12-week goal, write your 2 lead indicators. This Sunday, schedule next week's lead actions into your calendar like appointments.

lessons.title: The Scoreboard Makes It Real
lessons.summary: What gets measured gets managed — and what gets SEEN gets done. The 12 Week Year requires a public scoreboard: your weekly lead actions, visible and tracked, with a simple 'on track / off track' read. Public tracking creates the honesty loop: you can't quietly drift for three weeks and call it a year.
lessons.example: Moran's teams put scoreboards on office walls with a weekly tally; individuals keep theirs on the fridge or as a pinned note. The teams that kept the board visible hit their numbers; the ones that 'didn't have time' for the board didn't.
lessons.action: Create your scoreboard today: one page (paper or digital) with your lead actions and a checkbox per week. Put it where you'll see it daily.

lessons.title: Accountability: The Weekly Partner Meeting
lessons.summary: The final pillar is a weekly accountability session — 15–30 minutes with a partner (or a group) where you report your score: what you committed to, what you did, what you'll do next week. Knowing you'll report makes the week's choices sharper. Ownership is the flip side: you don't blame circumstances — you own the results and adjust the plan.
lessons.example: Moran reports that people in accountability groups complete dramatically more than solo planners — one executive who had never finished a fitness program finished 3 full 12-week cycles with a weekly partner call.
lessons.action: Find one accountability partner this week. Book a fixed 20-minute weekly call: report your scoreboard, commit to next week's lead actions.

lessons.title: Compress Your Year and Watch Execution Follow
lessons.summary: Moran and Lennington's premise: annual goals create annual urgency — you only feel the pressure in December. By treating twelve weeks as a year, you force the same ambition into a quarter, creating constant urgency and faster feedback loops. Short horizons convert strategy from a document into a rhythm.
lessons.example: Teams that switched to 12-week plans reported sharper priorities and fewer abandoned initiatives — a goal that felt comfortable over 12 months became actionable over 12 weeks. The compression doesn't change the work; it changes how seriously you take it.
lessons.action: Write your three most important goals with a 12-week deadline and a weekly review habit.

actionPlan: Pick one goal and give it an 84-day deadline.
Write your 100-word future-self letter; extract 3 measurable goals.
Define 2 lead indicators per goal — actions you control.
Build a visible weekly scoreboard and check it daily.
Book a weekly accountability call with a partner — and never miss it.
caveat: Moran's 'compress your year into 12 weeks' is the most intense productivity system ever — and Clubhouse is its warning: no company ever sprinted harder — a 12-week rocket from zero to 10 million users, celebrity rooms, a $4 billion valuation in under a year — and the sprint ended the moment the world reopened, because the system was built for intensity, not durability. A 12-week year works when you're building a business; Clubhouse built an event. Sprint cycles need a product that people still want in week 13.
